title: He didn’t run from the lion.
paragraphs:
He didn’t run from the lion.
He ran toward it.

On a snowy day.
Cold ground. Slippery pit. No witnesses. No applause.
Just a man… and a decision.
Benaiah.
One verse. One line. Almost hidden.
But heaven didn’t overlook it.
“He struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen.” — 2 Samuel 23:20
Read that again.

A lion.
A pit.
Snow.
Every condition screams retreat.
But Benaiah steps forward.
Why?

Because courage is not built in comfort.
It is forged in moments where obedience costs you everything.

Let me ask you something—
What lion have you been avoiding?

That private sin you keep excusing.
That calling you keep delaying.
That fear you keep baptizing as “wisdom.”
That addiction you swear you’ll quit “next time.”
Listen carefully.

Some lions grow stronger the longer you ignore them.
Some pits get deeper the more you hesitate.
And one day… what you refused to confront will start confronting you.

Benaiah didn’t negotiate with danger.
He didn’t wait for better weather.
He didn’t ask for backup.
He moved.

Not because he felt fearless—
But because he trusted God more than his fear.
And that’s where many of us get it wrong.

We think courage means the absence of fear.
No.
Courage is obedience in the presence of fear.

But here’s where the story shifts—
And this is where the Gospel explodes into the scene.
Because if we’re honest…
We are not naturally Benaiah.

We are the ones who hesitate.
We are the ones who hide.
We are the ones who fall.
Scripture says the enemy prowls like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5:8).
That’s not just poetry. That’s reality.

And left to ourselves?
We don’t chase lions.
We get trapped by them.

Sin.
Shame.
Guilt.
Addiction.
Pride.

These are not small animals.
These are predators.
And here is the truth that humbles us:
We needed someone to step into the pit for us.
Enter Jesus.

Not as a distant observer.
Not as a motivational speaker from the edge.
But as a Savior who steps down into our darkness.

He didn’t come on a sunny day.
He entered a broken world—cold, hostile, resistant.

He faced temptation head-on.
He confronted sin without compromise.
He stood before death itself.
And at the cross… it looked like the Lion had won.

Darkness covered the sky.
The Son of God was nailed, mocked, and buried.
Silence.
But three days later—
The grave couldn’t hold Him.
Jesus didn’t just fight the lion.
He crushed it.

Sin—defeated.
Death—broken.
Satan—disarmed.

This is not symbolism.
This is salvation.

So now, when you face your lion…
You are not fighting for victory.
You are fighting from victory.

Because of Jesus, you don’t face sin alone.
Because of Jesus, repentance is not shame—it’s freedom.
Because of Jesus, your pit is not your prison—it can become your turning point.
Benaiah’s story shows us courage.
Jesus’ story gives us power.
And here’s what happens next—

Benaiah, the man in the pit, becomes a man near the throne.
He later becomes commander of King David’s bodyguard (2 Samuel 23:22–23).
Do you see the pattern?

Faithfulness in hidden battles…
Leads to influence in visible places.
God watches what others ignore.

That fight you’re in right now?
That silent struggle no one applauds?
He sees it.

Every resisted temptation.
Every quiet prayer.
Every step of obedience when it would’ve been easier to quit.
He sees.

So don’t despise your snowy day.
Don’t curse your pit.
Don’t bow to your lion.
Bring it to Jesus.

Name it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
And then take one step of obedience—today.

Not tomorrow.
Not when it’s easier.
Not when you “feel ready.”
Today.
Because delayed obedience is still disobedience.
And your breakthrough might be on the other side of one hard, holy decision.
You are not overlooked.

God builds His fiercest warriors in hidden places.
He writes His strongest stories in unseen battles.
Benaiah reminds us that courage matters.
But Jesus?
Jesus is the reason courage is possible at all.
So rise.

Face your lion.
Step into your pit.
Stand on His victory.
And watch what God does with a life that refuses to run.
Someone you know is fighting a lion in silence.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
